title: Pauri 22, meaning: worlds beyond worlds
hookLine: underworlds beyond underworlds, skies beyond skies; if it could be written it would be, but the writing runs out (Japji 22)

cards: Every notebook has a last page. Somebody sets out to list everything visible from a hilltop: each roof, each tree, each bird. The first notebook fills, then a shelf of them.
The handwriting gets shaky, and the view hasn't gotten any smaller. The one writing runs out before the view does. Pauri 22 says something like that, and it isn't sad about it.
It's almost relieved: this was never going to fit on paper.

teach.b: After the underworlds and the skies, Pauri 22 goes on, in paraphrase. People searched and searched for the farthest edge, and grew tired. The Vedas say this one thing: there's no end to find.

teach.h: THE VEDAS, THE KATEB, ONE SOURCE.
teach.b: The Kateb, the books of the Semitic traditions, speak of eighteen thousand worlds; but at the root there is one source. Notice what Guru Nanak does.
He gathers the scriptures of the two communities around him, Hindu and Muslim, and hears them both pointing the same way: past counting, toward one. He doesn't set them against each other.

Then the line behind today's carry: lekhaa hoe ta likheeai lekhai hoe vinaas. If there were an account, you could write it down; but the account perishes in the writing. Lekhaa is an account, a ledger, a tally.
Vinaas is destruction, perishing. Commentators read it two ways: the account itself falls apart before it's done, or the one writing perishes before it's finished. Either way, the writing runs out.

teach.h: CALL HIM GREAT; HE KNOWS HIMSELF.
teach.b: The stanza ends, in paraphrase: Nanak says, call Him great; He alone knows Himself.
That's not giving up. It's the move Japji has made since Pauri 12, no pen for this, and it's the right size of a human being, standing under the sky. Anyone can say great.
No one can write the whole ledger.

how: Pauri 22 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs often cite its closing, that only the One knows Himself, when speaking of the limits of human description.

o: a holy book, like the Vedas or Kateb
a scribe who writes the records down
an account or ledger, a written tally

games.q: what's inside Pauri 22 — tap the pairs.
p: grew tired looking for the edge

s: Pauri 22 sets the Vedas and the Kateb against each other
it hears them both pointing past counting, toward one source.
Pauri 22 says the account perishes in the writing
lekhaa hoe ta likheeai lekhai hoe vinaas.
Pauri 22 ends: call Him great; He alone knows Himself
not giving up, but standing at the right size under the sky.

games.q: you set out to write the full account of every world. what does Pauri 22 say happens?
o: you finish it with enough notebooks.
the writing runs out before the worlds do.
you find the last world at the edge.
games.why: if there were an account, it would be written; but the account perishes in the writing. Nanak says: call Him great.

practice: If you can, look at the sky for a minute, through a window, from a doorway, or outside; if you can't see it, close your eyes and picture the widest sky you remember. Don't name or count what's there; just let it be bigger than you.
Then close your eyes and sit with the size of it.

wordCard.voice: Lekhaa, an account or ledger. Worlds beyond worlds; the searchers grow tired; if it could be written, it would be, but the writing runs out. Call Him great.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: lekhaa, an account or ledger; in Pauri 22, the account that perishes in the writing.

carryVoice: Your line: the writing runs out. The ledger stays unfinished, and the sky is still there to look at. That's day one hundred ninety-eight.
